8-1.title: Greek & Latin Roots and Affixes
8-1.learn:
HOW TO USE GREEK AND LATIN ROOTS AND AFFIXES

Many English words are built from a ROOT (the core meaning) plus a PREFIX (added to the front) or SUFFIX (added to the end). Knowing common word parts helps you figure out new words.

Common roots: tele- (far), -phone (sound), -port (carry), -scope (see), bio- (life), -graph (write), aqua- (water), -dict (say).
Common prefixes: re- (again), un- (not), pre- (before), tri- (three), sub- (under), trans- (across).
Common suffixes: -less (without), -ful (full of), -er (one who).

Example 1 — 'telephone' = tele (far) + phone (sound) = sound from far away.

Example 2 — 'transport' = trans (across) + port (carry) = to carry across.

Example 3 — 'biography' = bio (life) + graph (write) = a writing about someone's life.
Tip: Break an unknown word into parts. Match each part to a meaning you know, then put the meanings together to guess the word.

questions.question: The root 'tele-' means 'far.' What does 'telescope' help you do?

choices.A: See things that are far away

questions.explanation: 'Tele-' means far and '-scope' means see, so a telescope lets you see far away.

questions.question: The prefix 're-' means 'again.' What does 'rewrite' mean?

choices.A: To write for the first time

questions.explanation: The prefix 're-' means again, so 'rewrite' means to write again.

questions.question: The prefix 'un-' means 'not.' What does 'unhappy' mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' means not, so 'unhappy' means not happy.

questions.question: The root '-port' means 'carry.' What does 'portable' most likely mean?
questions.explanation: '-port' means carry, so 'portable' means able to be carried.

questions.question: The prefix 'tri-' means 'three.' How many sides does a 'triangle' have?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'tri-' means three, so a triangle has three sides.

questions.question: The root 'aqua-' means 'water.' What is an 'aquarium' most likely for?
questions.explanation: 'Aqua-' means water, so an aquarium is a tank that holds water and fish.

questions.question: The suffix '-less' means 'without.' What does 'fearless' mean?
questions.explanation: The suffix '-less' means without, so 'fearless' means without fear.

questions.question: The root '-dict' means 'say' or 'speak.' What does 'predict' most likely mean?

choices.A: To say something before it happens

questions.explanation: 'Pre-' means before and '-dict' means say, so 'predict' means to say something before it happens.

questions.question: Using roots, what does 'biography' (bio = life, graph = write) mean?
questions.explanation: 'Bio' means life and 'graph' means write, so a biography is a writing about someone's life.

questions.question: The prefix 'trans-' means 'across.' What does 'transcontinental' describe?
questions.explanation: 'Trans-' means across, so 'transcontinental' means going across a continent.

questions.question: The prefix 'pre-' means 'before.' What does 'preview' mean?

choices.B: To view before the main event

questions.explanation: 'Pre-' means before and 'view' means see, so a 'preview' is a look at something before the main event.

questions.question: The suffix '-ful' means 'full of.' What does 'joyful' mean?
questions.explanation: The suffix '-ful' means full of, so 'joyful' means full of joy.

questions.question: The prefix 'sub-' means 'under.' What does 'submarine' describe?

choices.A: A boat that travels under the water
choices.B: A boat that flies above land

questions.explanation: 'Sub-' means under and 'marine' relates to the sea, so a submarine travels under the water.

questions.question: The suffix '-er' can mean 'one who.' What is a 'teacher'?
questions.explanation: The suffix '-er' means one who, so a 'teacher' is one who teaches.

questions.question: The root '-phone' means 'sound.' What does a 'microphone' do?

choices.B: Picks up small sounds and makes them louder

questions.explanation: 'Micro-' means small and '-phone' means sound, so a microphone captures sound so it can be made louder.

questions.question: The prefix 'un-' means 'not.' What does 'unfair' mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' means not, so 'unfair' means not fair.

questions.question: The root '-graph' means 'write' or 'draw.' What does an 'autograph' most likely mean? (auto = self)
questions.explanation: 'Auto' means self and '-graph' means write, so an autograph is a person's own written signature.

questions.question: The prefix 'bi-' means 'two.' What does a 'bicycle' have?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'bi-' means two, so a bicycle has two wheels.

questions.question: The suffix '-less' means 'without.' What does 'helpless' mean?

choices.B: Without help or unable to help oneself

questions.explanation: The suffix '-less' means without, so 'helpless' means without help.

questions.question: The prefix 're-' means 'again.' What does 'reread' mean?

choices.A: To read for the first time

questions.explanation: The prefix 're-' means again, so 'reread' means to read something again.

questions.question: The root 'aqua-' means 'water.' What does 'aquatic' describe?
questions.explanation: 'Aqua-' means water, so 'aquatic' describes things that live or grow in water.

questions.question: The suffix '-ful' means 'full of.' What does 'careful' mean?
questions.explanation: The suffix '-ful' means full of, so 'careful' means full of care.

questions.question: The prefix 'mis-' means 'wrongly.' What does 'misspell' mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'mis-' means wrongly, so 'misspell' means to spell a word wrongly.

questions.question: The root '-scope' means 'see.' What does a 'microscope' do? (micro = small)

choices.A: Lets you see very small things

questions.explanation: 'Micro-' means small and '-scope' means see, so a microscope lets you see very small things.

questions.question: The prefix 'dis-' means 'not' or 'opposite of.' What does 'disagree' mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'dis-' means not or the opposite of, so 'disagree' means to not agree.

questions.question: The root 'thermo-' means 'heat.' What does a 'thermometer' do? (meter = measure)
questions.explanation: 'Thermo-' means heat and '-meter' means measure, so a thermometer measures heat, or temperature.

questions.question: The prefix 'inter-' means 'between' or 'among.' What does 'international' mean?
questions.explanation: 'Inter-' means between or among, so 'international' means between or among nations.

questions.question: The root '-dict' means 'say.' What does 'dictate' most likely mean?

choices.A: To say words aloud for someone to write down

questions.explanation: '-dict' means say, so 'dictate' means to say words aloud, often for someone else to write down.

questions.question: Using word parts, what does 'biology' mean? (bio = life, -logy = study of)
questions.explanation: 'Bio' means life and '-logy' means study of, so biology is the study of living things.

questions.question: The prefix 'anti-' means 'against.' What does an 'antibacterial' soap do?
questions.explanation: 'Anti-' means against, so an antibacterial soap works against bacteria.

questions.question: The root '-port' means 'carry.' What does 'export' most likely mean? (ex- = out)

choices.A: To carry goods out of a country to sell
choices.C: To store goods in a warehouse

questions.explanation: 'Ex-' means out and '-port' means carry, so 'export' means to carry goods out of a country.

questions.question: The prefix 'tri-' means 'three.' What is a 'tripod'?
questions.explanation: 'Tri-' means three and 'pod' refers to feet or legs, so a tripod is a three-legged stand.

questions.question: The prefix 'un-' means 'not.' What does 'unknown' mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' means not, so 'unknown' means not known.

questions.question: The suffix '-er' can mean 'one who.' What is a 'painter'?
questions.explanation: The suffix '-er' means one who, so a 'painter' is one who paints.

questions.question: The prefix 're-' means 'again.' What does 'rebuild' mean?
questions.explanation: The prefix 're-' means again, so 'rebuild' means to build again.

questions.question: The root 'geo-' means 'earth.' What does 'geography' study? (-graph = write/describe)
questions.explanation: 'Geo-' means earth, so geography is the study and description of the earth and its features.

questions.question: The suffix '-able' means 'able to be.' What does 'readable' mean?
questions.explanation: The suffix '-able' means able to be, so 'readable' means able to be read.

questions.question: The prefix 'pre-' means 'before.' What does 'preheat' mean?

choices.B: To heat ahead of time, before you need it

questions.explanation: 'Pre-' means before, so 'preheat' means to heat ahead of time, before it is needed.

questions.question: Using word parts, what does 'telegraph' mean? (tele = far, graph = write)

choices.A: A tool for seeing far away
choices.D: A device for writing messages over a far distance

questions.explanation: 'Tele-' means far and '-graph' means write, so a telegraph sends written messages over a far distance.

questions.question: The root '-spect' means 'look' or 'see.' What does 'inspect' most likely mean? (in- = into)
questions.explanation: 'In-' means into and '-spect' means look, so 'inspect' means to look carefully into something.

8-2.title: Using Context Clues
8-2.learn:
HOW TO USE CONTEXT CLUES

When you meet an unfamiliar word, look at the nearby words for hints. Four common kinds of context clues:
- DEFINITION: the meaning is stated nearby ('A meteorologist, a scientist who studies weather, gave the forecast.')
- EXAMPLE: examples show the meaning ('Citrus fruits, such as oranges and lemons, are sour.')
- SYNONYM: a word with a similar meaning is nearby ('She was elated, or very happy.')
- CONTRAST/ANTONYM: an opposite word gives a hint ('Unlike his timid brother, Max was bold.')

Example 1 — 'The arid desert had no water for miles.'
The words 'desert' and 'no water' tell you 'arid' means dry.

Example 2 — 'He was reluctant to go; he really did not want to leave home.'
'Did not want to' tells you 'reluctant' means unwilling.

Example 3 — 'Unlike the noisy crowd, the library was tranquil.'
The contrast with 'noisy' tells you 'tranquil' means calm and quiet.
Tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue words, and let them point you to the meaning.

questions.question: Read: 'The arid desert had no water for miles.' What does 'arid' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'desert' and 'no water' show that 'arid' means dry.

questions.question: Read: 'She was elated, or very happy, about her award.' What does 'elated' mean?
questions.explanation: The synonym clue 'or very happy' tells you that 'elated' means very happy.

questions.question: Read: 'Citrus fruits, such as oranges and lemons, are sour.' What are 'citrus fruits'?

choices.B: Sour fruits like oranges and lemons

questions.explanation: The example clue 'such as oranges and lemons' shows what citrus fruits are.

questions.question: Read: 'He was reluctant to go; he really did not want to leave home.' What does 'reluctant' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'did not want to' tells you 'reluctant' means unwilling.

questions.question: Read: 'Unlike his timid brother, Max was bold and fearless.' What does 'timid' mean?
questions.explanation: The contrast with 'bold and fearless' shows that 'timid' means shy or fearful.

questions.question: Read: 'The vast ocean stretched as far as the eye could see.' What does 'vast' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'as far as the eye could see' shows that 'vast' means huge.

questions.question: What kind of context clue is used in 'A glacier, a giant sheet of slow-moving ice, carved the valley'?
questions.explanation: The phrase 'a giant sheet of slow-moving ice' directly defines the word 'glacier.'

questions.question: Read: 'The detective was meticulous, checking every tiny detail with great care.' What does 'meticulous' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'checking every tiny detail with great care' shows 'meticulous' means very careful and precise.

questions.question: Read: 'While the others were boisterous, Anna stayed calm and quiet.' What does 'boisterous' mean?
questions.explanation: The contrast with 'calm and quiet' shows that 'boisterous' means loud and rowdy.

questions.question: Read: 'The bridge was so dilapidated that boards were missing and the rails had rusted away.' What does 'dilapidated' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'boards were missing' and 'rails had rusted away' show 'dilapidated' means broken down and in ruin.

questions.question: Read: 'The soup was bland, so Dad added salt and pepper to give it some flavor.' What does 'bland' mean?
questions.explanation: Because Dad had to add salt and pepper for flavor, 'bland' means having little flavor.

questions.question: Read: 'The puppy was energetic, running and jumping all around the yard.' What does 'energetic' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'running and jumping all around' shows 'energetic' means full of energy and active.

questions.question: Read: 'The instructions were so complex that no one could follow them.' What does 'complex' mean?
questions.explanation: Because no one could follow them, 'complex' means complicated and hard to understand.

questions.question: Read: 'Predators, such as wolves and hawks, hunt other animals for food.' What are 'predators'?
questions.explanation: The example clue 'such as wolves and hawks' that 'hunt other animals' shows predators are hunting animals.

questions.question: Read: 'The gloomy sky was gray and heavy with rain clouds.' What does 'gloomy' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'gray' and 'heavy with rain clouds' show that 'gloomy' means dark and dreary.

questions.question: Read: 'She was generous, always sharing her snacks and helping others.' What does 'generous' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'always sharing and helping others' shows 'generous' means willing to give and share.

questions.question: Read: 'Unlike the fresh bread, the old loaf was stale and hard.' What does 'stale' mean?

choices.C: No longer fresh; old and dry

questions.explanation: The contrast with 'fresh bread' shows that 'stale' means no longer fresh.

questions.question: Read: 'The teacher's voice was audible, easy for everyone in the back row to hear.' What does 'audible' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'easy for everyone to hear' shows that 'audible' means able to be heard.

questions.question: What kind of context clue is used in 'She felt jubilant, or extremely joyful, on graduation day'?
questions.explanation: The phrase 'or extremely joyful' gives a synonym, so this is a synonym clue.

questions.question: Read: 'The room was immaculate; not a single speck of dust could be found.' What does 'immaculate' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'not a single speck of dust' shows that 'immaculate' means perfectly clean.

questions.question: Read: 'The hikers were exhausted after the long climb and could barely walk.' What does 'exhausted' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'after the long climb and could barely walk' shows that 'exhausted' means very tired.

questions.question: Read: 'Whereas the first plan was vague, the second was specific and detailed.' What does 'vague' mean?
questions.explanation: The contrast with 'specific and detailed' shows that 'vague' means unclear or not detailed.

questions.question: Read: 'The crowd was enormous, filling every seat in the giant stadium.' What does 'enormous' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'filling every seat in the giant stadium' shows that 'enormous' means very large.

questions.question: Read: 'The crops withered and died because of the drought, a long period with no rain.' What does 'drought' mean?

choices.B: A long period with no rain

questions.explanation: The definition clue 'a long period with no rain' directly explains 'drought.'

questions.question: Read: 'The shy student was reticent, rarely speaking up in class.' What does 'reticent' mean?

choices.B: Quiet and not willing to speak

questions.explanation: The clues 'shy' and 'rarely speaking up' show that 'reticent' means quiet and not willing to speak.

questions.question: Read: 'The new policy was beneficial; it helped students and improved their grades.' What does 'beneficial' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'helped students and improved their grades' show that 'beneficial' means helpful.

questions.question: Read: 'Although the path looked treacherous, with loose rocks and steep drops, they pressed on.' What does 'treacherous' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'loose rocks and steep drops' show that 'treacherous' means dangerous.

questions.question: Read: 'The scientist's claim was dubious, and many doubted whether it could be true.' What does 'dubious' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'many doubted whether it could be true' shows that 'dubious' means doubtful or questionable.

questions.question: Read: 'In contrast to the lively party next door, our house was utterly placid that evening.' What does 'placid' mean?
questions.explanation: The contrast with the 'lively party' shows that 'placid' means calm and peaceful.

questions.question: Read: 'The volcano was dormant; it had not erupted or shown any activity for centuries.' What does 'dormant' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'had not erupted or shown any activity' shows that 'dormant' means inactive or sleeping.

questions.question: Read: 'The smell was so pungent that it stung our noses the moment we walked in.' What does 'pungent' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'stung our noses' shows that 'pungent' means a sharp, strong smell.

questions.question: Read: 'The directions were concise, just three short steps and nothing extra.' What does 'concise' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'three short steps and nothing extra' shows that 'concise' means short and to the point.

questions.question: Read: 'The toddler was inquisitive, asking question after question about everything she saw.' What does 'inquisitive' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'asking question after question' shows that 'inquisitive' means curious and full of questions.

questions.question: What kind of context clue is used in 'Mammals, such as dogs, whales, and bats, feed milk to their young'?
questions.explanation: The phrase 'such as dogs, whales, and bats' gives examples, so this is an example clue.

questions.question: Read: 'The diligent worker never stopped, finishing every task on time.' What does 'diligent' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'never stopped' and 'finishing every task on time' show that 'diligent' means hardworking.

questions.question: Read: 'Unlike the abundant apples on the full tree, the pears were scarce and hard to find.' What does 'scarce' mean?

choices.B: Hard to find; in short supply

questions.explanation: The contrast with 'abundant' apples shows that 'scarce' means hard to find or in short supply.

questions.question: Read: 'The lecture was monotonous, droning on in the same flat tone until students dozed off.' What does 'monotonous' mean?
questions.explanation: The clues 'same flat tone' and 'students dozed off' show that 'monotonous' means dull and unchanging.

questions.question: Read: 'The chef garnished the plate, adding a sprig of parsley and a lemon slice to decorate it.' What does 'garnished' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'adding parsley and a lemon slice to decorate' shows that 'garnished' means decorated with small touches.

questions.question: Read: 'The coach was adamant about practice and refused to change her mind no matter what.' What does 'adamant' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'refused to change her mind' shows that 'adamant' means firm and unwilling to change.

questions.question: Read: 'The lake was so murky that we could not see even an inch below the surface.' What does 'murky' mean?
questions.explanation: The clue 'could not see even an inch below the surface' shows that 'murky' means dark and cloudy.

8-3.title: Figurative Language in Your Writing
8-3.learn:
HOW TO RECOGNIZE FIGURATIVE LANGUAGE

Figurative language paints pictures with words instead of being literal. The main types:
- SIMILE: compares two things using 'like' or 'as' ('brave as a lion,' 'runs like the wind').
- METAPHOR: says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as' ('the classroom was a zoo').
- PERSONIFICATION: gives human traits to objects, animals, or ideas ('the wind whispered,' 'the sun smiled').
- HYPERBOLE: an extreme exaggeration ('I've told you a million times').

Example 1 — Simile: 'Her smile was as bright as the sun.'
It uses 'as' to compare her smile to the sun.

Example 2 — Metaphor: 'Time is a thief.'
It says time IS a thief (not 'like' a thief), so it is a metaphor.

Example 3 — Personification: 'The leaves danced in the wind.'
Leaves can't really dance — a human action is given to them.
Tip: 'like'/'as' = simile; direct 'is/was' comparison = metaphor; human action for non-human = personification; huge exaggeration = hyperbole.

questions.question: Which sentence is a SIMILE?

choices.A: Her smile was as bright as the sun.
choices.B: Her smile was a ray of sunshine.
choices.C: The sun smiled down on us.

questions.explanation: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; here 'as bright as the sun' is a simile.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR?

choices.D: She is as quiet as a mouse.

questions.explanation: A metaphor says one thing IS another without 'like' or 'as'; the classroom 'was a zoo.'

questions.question: Which sentence uses PERSONIFICATION?

choices.A: The car was as fast as lightning.
choices.B: The old engine coughed and groaned.
choices.C: He was a lion in battle.
choices.D: The road was long and straight.

questions.explanation: Giving the engine human actions ('coughed and groaned') is personification.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The stars danced in the night sky'?
questions.explanation: Stars cannot literally dance; giving them a human action is personification.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'My backpack weighs a ton'?
questions.explanation: It is an extreme exaggeration (the backpack doesn't really weigh a ton), so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: Which sentence is a SIMILE?

choices.A: The snow was a soft blanket.
choices.B: The snow fell like tiny feathers.

questions.explanation: 'Like tiny feathers' uses 'like' to compare, which makes it a simile.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'Time is a thief'?
questions.explanation: It directly says time IS a thief (no 'like' or 'as'), making it a metaphor.

questions.question: Which sentence uses figurative language, NOT a literal statement?

choices.A: The dog ran across the yard.

questions.explanation: Giving the thunder the human emotion of grumbling angrily is personification, a kind of figurative language.

questions.question: Read: 'The classroom buzzed like a beehive during the project.' What type of figurative language is this?
questions.explanation: It compares the classroom to a beehive using 'like,' so it is a simile.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR (not a simile)?

choices.A: Life is a roller coaster of ups and downs.
choices.B: Life is like a roller coaster.
choices.C: Her hair was as black as night.

questions.explanation: A metaphor states one thing IS another without 'like' or 'as'; 'Life is a roller coaster' does this.

questions.question: Which sentence is a SIMILE?

choices.A: He was a brave lion in battle.
choices.D: He was as brave as a lion.

questions.explanation: 'As brave as a lion' uses 'as' to compare, making it a simile.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'I have a million things to do today'?
questions.explanation: Nobody really has a million things to do; it is an exaggeration, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: Which sentence uses PERSONIFICATION?

choices.A: The alarm clock screamed at me to wake up.
choices.B: The alarm clock was as loud as a siren.
choices.D: I turned off the alarm clock.

questions.explanation: An alarm clock cannot really scream; giving it that human action is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR?

choices.B: Her eyes were two shining diamonds.

questions.explanation: It says her eyes WERE diamonds (no 'like' or 'as'), making it a metaphor.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'as cold as ice'?
questions.explanation: It compares using 'as,' so 'as cold as ice' is a simile.

questions.question: Which sentence uses HYPERBOLE?

choices.A: This box is a little heavy.
choices.B: This box weighs more than a thousand elephants!

questions.explanation: Weighing 'more than a thousand elephants' is an extreme exaggeration, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The flowers nodded their heads in the breeze'?
questions.explanation: Flowers cannot really nod their heads; giving them that human action is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence is a SIMILE?

choices.A: The water was a sheet of glass.
choices.B: The water was as smooth as glass.
choices.C: The water rippled in the wind.
choices.D: We swam in the cold water.

questions.explanation: 'As smooth as glass' uses 'as' to compare, so it is a simile.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The world is a stage'?
questions.explanation: It says the world IS a stage with no 'like' or 'as,' so it is a metaphor.

questions.question: Which sentence uses HYPERBOLE?

choices.A: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse.

questions.explanation: Being hungry enough to 'eat a horse' is an extreme exaggeration, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The sun greeted us with its warm rays'?
questions.explanation: The sun cannot really greet anyone; giving it that human action is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR?

choices.A: The night sky is a blanket of stars.
choices.B: The night sky was like a blanket.

questions.explanation: It says the sky IS a blanket of stars (no 'like' or 'as'), so it is a metaphor.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a SIMILE?

choices.A: My brother eats like a pig.
choices.B: My brother is a pig at dinner.
choices.D: The pig ran around the farm.

questions.explanation: 'Eats like a pig' uses 'like' to compare, making it a simile.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The angry clouds threatened the city below'?
questions.explanation: Clouds cannot feel anger or threaten; giving them human traits is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence uses HYPERBOLE?

choices.A: My grandmother is older than dirt.
choices.B: My grandmother is sixty years old.

questions.explanation: Being 'older than dirt' is an impossible exaggeration, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'as busy as a bee'?
questions.explanation: It compares using 'as,' so 'as busy as a bee' is a simile.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR?

choices.A: The test was a piece of cake.
choices.B: The test was as easy as cake.
choices.C: We ate cake after the test.

questions.explanation: It says the test WAS a piece of cake (no 'like' or 'as'), so it is a metaphor.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The waves crashed and the sea roared with fury'?
questions.explanation: Giving the sea the human emotion of fury is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence is a SIMILE?

choices.B: His temper erupted like a volcano.

questions.explanation: 'Erupted like a volcano' uses 'like' to compare, so it is a simile.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'I've asked you a thousand times to clean your room'?
questions.explanation: 'A thousand times' is an exaggeration to make a point, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR?

choices.A: Her bedroom is a disaster zone.
choices.B: Her bedroom is like a disaster zone.

questions.explanation: It says her bedroom IS a disaster zone (no 'like' or 'as'), so it is a metaphor.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The hungry fire ate through the dry forest'?
questions.explanation: Fire cannot be hungry or eat; giving it those human traits is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a SIMILE?

choices.D: The baby's skin was as soft as silk.

questions.explanation: 'As soft as silk' uses 'as' to compare, making it a simile.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'My feet are killing me'?
questions.explanation: Feet cannot really kill anyone; it is an exaggeration of pain, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: Which sentence is a METAPHOR?

choices.A: The snow is a white blanket over the hills.
choices.B: The snow looks like a white blanket.

questions.explanation: It says the snow IS a white blanket (no 'like' or 'as'), so it is a metaphor.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'The leaves whispered secrets as we passed'?
questions.explanation: Leaves cannot whisper secrets; giving them that human action is personification.

questions.question: Which sentence uses figurative language, NOT a literal statement?

choices.B: The runner was a streak of lightning down the track.
choices.D: The track is four hundred meters.

questions.explanation: Calling the runner 'a streak of lightning' is a metaphor, a kind of figurative language.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'as light as a feather'?
questions.explanation: It compares using 'as,' so 'as light as a feather' is a simile.

questions.question: Which sentence uses HYPERBOLE?

choices.A: It took forever and a day to finish the chores.
choices.D: Chores are part of my routine.

questions.explanation: 'Forever and a day' is an extreme exaggeration of time, so it is hyperbole.

questions.question: What type of figurative language is 'Opportunity knocked, and she opened the door'?
questions.explanation: Opportunity is an idea and cannot knock; giving it a human action is personification.

8-4.title: Connotation vs. Denotation
8-4.learn:
HOW TO TELL CONNOTATION FROM DENOTATION

DENOTATION is a word's exact dictionary meaning. CONNOTATION is the FEELING or emotion a word carries — positive, negative, or neutral.

Example 1 — 'thrifty' vs. 'cheap.'
Both have the denotation 'spending little money.' But 'thrifty' has a POSITIVE connotation (smart with money), while 'cheap' has a NEGATIVE connotation (stingy).

Example 2 — 'slender,' 'thin,' 'skinny.'
All mean 'not heavy' (denotation). 'Slender' sounds positive, 'thin' sounds neutral, and 'skinny' can sound negative.

Example 3 — 'curious' vs. 'nosy.'
Both mean 'interested in others' business.' 'Curious' is positive; 'nosy' is negative.
Tip: Two words can share a denotation but feel very different. To pick the right word, decide whether you want a positive, neutral, or negative feeling — that's choosing the right connotation for your tone.

questions.question: What is the DENOTATION of a word?
questions.explanation: Denotation is a word's exact dictionary meaning.

questions.question: What is the CONNOTATION of a word?

choices.C: The feeling or emotion it carries

questions.explanation: Connotation is the feeling or emotion a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning.

questions.question: Which word has a POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Thrifty' suggests being smart with money, giving it a positive connotation.

questions.question: Which word has a NEGATIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Scrawny' suggests being unhealthily thin, giving it a negative connotation.

questions.question: 'Curious' and 'nosy' share a similar meaning. Which has the more POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Curious' sounds positive (eager to learn), while 'nosy' sounds negative (prying).

questions.question: Which word would you choose to describe a leader in a POSITIVE way?
questions.explanation: 'Confident' carries a positive connotation, while 'bossy,' 'pushy,' and 'demanding' sound negative.

questions.question: Which pair of words shares the same DENOTATION but different connotations?
questions.explanation: 'Famous' and 'notorious' both mean well-known, but 'famous' is positive and 'notorious' is negative.

questions.question: A writer wants to describe a determined character POSITIVELY. Which word fits best?
questions.explanation: 'Persistent' has a positive connotation, while 'stubborn,' 'bullheaded,' and 'obstinate' sound negative.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a word with a NEGATIVE connotation to shape the tone?

choices.A: The aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen.
choices.B: The stench of old garbage filled the alley.
choices.C: The scent of flowers drifted by.
choices.D: The smell of rain was refreshing.

questions.explanation: 'Stench' carries a strongly negative connotation, unlike the more pleasant or neutral 'aroma,' 'scent,' and 'smell.'

questions.question: Why might a writer choose 'inexpensive' instead of 'cheap' to describe a product?

choices.B: Because 'inexpensive' has a more positive connotation, even though both mean low-cost

questions.explanation: Both words mean low-cost (same denotation), but 'inexpensive' sounds positive while 'cheap' can sound poorly made.

questions.question: 'Young' and 'childish' can both describe someone who is not grown up. Which has the more NEGATIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Childish' carries a negative feeling (immature), while 'young' is neutral or positive.

questions.question: Which word has a POSITIVE connotation for someone who talks a lot?
questions.explanation: 'Articulate' praises someone who speaks well, giving it a positive connotation; 'blabbermouth' is clearly negative.

questions.question: 'Aroma' and 'odor' can both mean a smell. Which has the more POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Aroma' suggests a pleasant smell (positive), while 'odor' often suggests an unpleasant one.

questions.question: Which word would describe a quiet person in a POSITIVE way?
questions.explanation: 'Reserved' is a respectful, positive way to describe someone quiet; the others sound negative.

questions.question: Which word has a NEGATIVE connotation for someone who is not spending much?
questions.explanation: 'Miserly' suggests being unpleasantly tight with money (negative); the others sound positive or neutral.

questions.question: 'Slim' and 'gaunt' both describe a thin person. Which has the more NEGATIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Gaunt' suggests an unhealthy, bony thinness (negative), while 'slim' sounds attractive and positive.

questions.question: Which word would you choose to praise a clever person POSITIVELY?
questions.explanation: 'Resourceful' is a positive way to call someone clever; 'sneaky,' 'scheming,' and 'cunning' carry negative feelings.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a word with a POSITIVE connotation?

choices.A: The crowd of fans was a mob.
choices.B: The crowd of fans was a gang.
choices.C: The crowd of fans gathered eagerly.
choices.D: The crowd of fans was a horde.

questions.explanation: 'Gathered eagerly' sounds positive, while 'mob,' 'gang,' and 'horde' carry negative connotations for a crowd.

questions.question: Two words have the SAME denotation but different connotations. Which pair is an example?
questions.explanation: 'Relaxed' and 'lazy' both mean not active, but 'relaxed' is positive and 'lazy' is negative.

questions.question: Which word would describe a strong-smelling, pleasant perfume in a POSITIVE way?
questions.explanation: 'Fragrance' has a pleasant, positive connotation; 'reek,' 'stink,' and 'funk' are negative.

questions.question: 'Unique' and 'weird' can both describe something unusual. Which has the more POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Unique' sounds special and positive, while 'weird' sounds strange and negative.

questions.question: Which word would you choose to describe a child's energy POSITIVELY?
questions.explanation: 'Lively' is a positive way to describe energy; 'hyper,' 'wild,' and 'out of control' sound negative.

questions.question: Which word has a NEGATIVE connotation for someone who is sure of themselves?
questions.explanation: 'Arrogant' suggests too much pride (negative), while 'confident,' 'self-assured,' and 'poised' sound positive.

questions.question: 'Group' and 'clique' can both name a set of friends. Which has the more NEGATIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Clique' suggests an exclusive, unfriendly group (negative), while 'group' is neutral.

questions.question: Which word would describe an old house POSITIVELY?
questions.explanation: 'Historic' gives an old house a positive feeling of value; 'rundown,' 'shabby,' and 'decrepit' are negative.

questions.question: Which word has a POSITIVE connotation for a person who does not give up?
questions.explanation: 'Determined' praises someone who keeps trying (positive); 'pushy' and 'nagging' are negative.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a word with a NEGATIVE connotation?

choices.A: The chef created a special dish.
choices.B: The chef concocted a strange dish.
choices.C: The chef prepared a special dish.
choices.D: The chef cooked a special dish.

questions.explanation: 'Concocted a strange dish' carries a negative, suspicious feeling, unlike the neutral 'created,' 'prepared,' and 'cooked.'

questions.question: 'Slender' and 'lanky' can both describe a tall, thin person. Which has the more POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Slender' sounds graceful and positive, while 'lanky' suggests awkward thinness.

questions.question: Which word would you choose to praise an inexpensive but well-made item POSITIVELY?
questions.explanation: 'Affordable' has a positive connotation for low price; 'cheap,' 'shoddy,' and 'flimsy' suggest poor quality.

questions.question: Which word has a NEGATIVE connotation for someone who is careful with details?
questions.explanation: 'Picky' has a negative feeling (hard to please), while 'thorough,' 'precise,' and 'careful' are positive.

questions.question: 'Childlike' and 'childish' both relate to children. Which has the more POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Childlike' suggests innocence and wonder (positive), while 'childish' suggests immaturity (negative).

questions.question: Which word would describe a strong smell of food in a POSITIVE way?
questions.explanation: 'Aroma' suggests a pleasant food smell (positive); 'stench' and 'reek' are negative.

questions.question: Which word has a POSITIVE connotation for a person who saves money?
questions.explanation: 'Frugal' is a positive way to describe a careful saver; the others sound negative.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a word with a POSITIVE connotation to describe a thin model?

choices.A: The skinny model walked the runway.
choices.B: The bony model walked the runway.
choices.C: The slim model walked the runway.
choices.D: The scrawny model walked the runway.

questions.explanation: 'Slim' has a positive, flattering connotation, while 'skinny,' 'bony,' and 'scrawny' sound negative.

questions.question: 'Smile' and 'smirk' both involve the mouth turning up. Which has the more NEGATIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Smirk' suggests a smug or unkind expression (negative), while 'smile' is warm and positive.

questions.question: Which word would describe a curious person POSITIVELY?
questions.explanation: 'Inquisitive' is a positive word for curiosity; 'nosy,' 'prying,' and 'snooping' are negative.

questions.question: Which word has a NEGATIVE connotation for someone who is relaxed about rules?
questions.explanation: 'Careless' suggests not caring enough (negative), while 'easygoing,' 'laid-back,' and 'calm' sound positive.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a word with a NEGATIVE connotation for a leader?

choices.A: The captain guided the team to victory.
choices.B: The captain led the team to victory.
choices.C: The captain dominated the team into victory.
choices.D: The captain inspired the team to victory.

questions.explanation: 'Dominated' carries a harsh, negative feeling, while 'guided,' 'led,' and 'inspired' sound positive.

questions.question: 'Pleasingly plump' and 'overweight' can both describe a heavier person. Which has the more POSITIVE connotation?
questions.explanation: 'Pleasingly plump' adds a kind, positive feeling, while 'overweight' is more clinical or negative.

questions.question: Why might a news writer call a protest a 'demonstration' rather than a 'riot'?

choices.A: Because the two words are unrelated
choices.B: Because 'demonstration' has a calmer, more positive connotation than the violent-sounding 'riot'

questions.explanation: Both can describe a gathering, but 'demonstration' sounds peaceful and positive while 'riot' sounds violent and negative.
